Orwell is one of those "your choices guide the game" games, but it's really unclear which of your choices cause what outcome, until the very last choice of the game. The only mechanic is to drag and drop snippets of text, it's all drowned within other useless text that you don't need to read, and I'd be awfully boring if you did. You're basically mindlessly dragging and dropping text until something happens and it's apparently your fault because you dragged some snippet of text, but who knows which one it was. To make it worse, sometimes you NEED to drag a certain snippet to progress the game, even if you're trying to make the choice not to, and finding that snippet is difficult among the other boring text. Progression of the story, especially the chats, was painfully slow. Finally, the characters are unloveable and the whole thing can be finished in ~2 hours but the story is so bland that you don't even know what happened.
Give this a try!

[h1][i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye One You’s[/i] centrism recklessly justifies surveillance[/h1]

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] (Osmotic Studios, 2016) should not have to prove that mass surveillance is a public danger. Lifting the name of one of the 20th century’s most enduring authors, [i]Orwell[/i] reverses the traditional dystopian power dynamic by casting the player as an investigator utilizing government software to snoop on anyone deemed potentially dangerous to the state. The setup is almost too clean to be proper satire, too on the nose to spark the outrage necessary to criticize what is fast becoming a common aspect of life.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality.

[i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination.

Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged.

But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power.

In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving.

The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance.

This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case?

[i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it.

Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down.

I think Orwell as a game is a great concept, but could have been executed far better. The game highlights important information, and railroads you into making choices that aren't backed by evidence. It doesn't provide enough detail for you to make judgement calls, but leaves you between two equally plausible answers, and forces you to make a choice. A better way of doing this would have been to present more information than necessary, and let players sort out what's important, and take their own notes. I would have preferred the game to involve less bias - letting players make their own choices, and come to their own conclusion on the benefits - or invasions - of government surveillance. I also feel the ending was robbed from me. I simply couldn't figure out how to support the cause of Thought, and wanted to have to face the ethical dilemma of doing so. Instead, I had to give them in as the only way to move forward. I really wanted to like this game, but I ultimately can't recommend it.

Let's say that all your social media posts from all your accounts were tied back to you. Everything that you have ever said, liked, or shared was being compiled to build a profile on you. Now imagine that this profile is being used to determine if you're a threat to society. Once information is put in, it cannot be removed. And it is entirely up to a single person's opinions to determine who you are.
Fun, story driven, and interactive. A great way to burn ~8 hours on a single play through, although you'll have to go back again to see the multiple endings.

So, more disappointing than fulfilling.

OK - to start with the bad; the way progression works is, to say the least, not exactly flawless. At multiple times I felt I had no choice but to do the exact opposite of what my intuition really led me towards, because if the story hasn't moved forward in a while, and you've already done everything that seems sensible, you've no real choice but to just take random stabs. You never know what will push the game to move the story forward, and unfortunately it can really weaken the immersion when you're going back to accept data points you had previously ruled out just on the off chance one of them will finally trigger the script to move forward.

Also, it sometimes feels a little restrictive that you are never freely choosing what information to select for processing - rather, you are selecting which of the automatically flagged information to process. So, sometimes it simply doesn't highlight something which might seem important to you, and sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information flagged isn't quite what you expected. To some extent, these can be forgiven as contributing to the theme that you are not entirely in control of the "Orwell" program, but nonetheless, this can also pull you out of the game if something really catches your attention but the lack of a flag is effectively the game telling you to ignore it.

Those minor irks aside, though - I actually thought this game was very good.

The story is interesting, and generally does an excellent job of avoiding lazy narrative tropes or character stereotypes. The combination of inferring information from investigating documents and reading call or chat transcripts as a means of piecing together events is used to excellent effect. Overall, the story is easily engaging enough to keep you invested in the game throughout, wanting to untangle all the details. 

The mechanics, despite the little irks I mentioned at the beginning of the review, also work really nicely on the whole. They feel genuinely fresh and original, and effectively encourage you to keep paying attention while working through a fairly hefty pile of documents.

I also appreciate that your choices make some meaningful differences, and the story is a manageable enough length that upon finishing my first run I immediately started another to try to reach the other outcomes. However, the repeat playthroughs to see the other possibilities play out weren't remotely enjoyable... The amount of identical information you have to grind through easily outweighs any enjoyment form seeing the alternative paths.

So, only worth playing through once, and not particularly long - but for the duration of that first playthrough, it's an interesting game with original mechanics and the story holds your attention.

I wouldn't pay full price, but if there's a decent discount I'd certainly recommend checking it out.

After finishing reading George Orwell's 1984, I think it would be better to understand the title of each chapter in a clearer perspective. I personally believe that such surveillance systems used to collect individual information must exist in many nations around the globe. There is a character, Harrison O'Donnell, who leaves a vivid and unforgettable impression on me. [spoiler] He is just a veil and hypocritical creep, writing columns for the official media while secretly scheming actions toward the government. [/spoiler] I am pretty sure that similar situations could be actually observed in daily life. Perhaps that might just represent the idea of "Doublethink" mentioned in 1984. However, I would still like to regard the behavior of being two-faced as hypocrisy and it should be condemned, but in a less aggressive way. As for the existence of the system, I have to admit its important function and efficiency to prevent certain people from doing harm to the public. On the other hand, I do consider it an offensive to human rights and privacy. Some may argue that compared with social security, individuals can be sometimes put aside. I will not accept it, for putting the two substances into comparison does not make any sense. If one suffered the bitter consequences of sacrificing individual privacy, then any of us would inevitably have the same likelihood to be victims as well. [spoiler] Moreover, Juliet, who wants to achieve her goals in a rather lethal method, has become an actual terrorist. [/spoiler] Her experience reminds me of the famous quote by Nietzsche, which can be seen at the very beginning of this review. Unfortunately, Juliet herself has failed to do that.

This is a great game that dares to explore the surveillance state.  The game play is pretty simple, you just dig around in peoples' social media to gather information which can be used to incriminate them, predict where to find them, predict where terrorist attacks could occur, etc.  You get to determine when something said is just hyperbole, or a real threat.  And your choices have consequences.  The music is pretty engaging.  There's no "action" though, its just not that type of game.

There are a number of "OMG" moments that spring up.  In light of real world events, like people in Europe being jailed for offensive social media posts, and China's social credit score and Project Dragonfly where what you post dictates if you can even buy a train ticket.... the game takes a necessary look into how political forces use social media for good and for ill.  It raises very real questions and awareness of just how screwed we'd all be without freedom of speech, as "anything" can be used to incriminate.  

I could not discern any political bias.  Whether conservative or liberal, I think both sides will be able to identify with the struggles, conversations and events that unfold.  Underneath it all we're all very much more alike than different.

Investigating terrorist activity from the shadows! This game really makes you feel like an FBI / NSA agent. It's really good! Fun thing is, this isn't far off from what's already happening all over the world. Instead of using a centralised guidance system, "Open Source Intelligence" investigators simply use their own means plus everything the open internet has to offer to analyse even the most innocent-seeming information shards. Look it up, it's called OSInt, you'll be surprised what they can do with even the most innocuous looking data.

The sense of realism they went for worked and got me to really sink into this world. The end is a bit off beat. There's a twist that just foregoes realism in favour of a over-the-top, grand conclusion. That aside though, it's a really great experience and I heartily recommend it to anyone with a passing interest in digital forensics.

I want to briefly discuss branching paths in this game. There are plenty of them, but unlike other games they are not straightforward choices like with typical dialog options. Instead it's a sequence of choices that you make that add up to a result branching in either direction. But for many of the choices you're not given any indication that they are in fact involved in a branching path. This makes it more realistic, but you'll need to keep in mind that although the game let's you process all digital information and out of curiosity you might (like me) want to postpone your decisions until you've processed them all, you will miss out on several branching paths, not realising that processing some innocuous looking data shards you actually forced yourself down a certain path. Once you figure out how rich this game is in its branching paths, you'll be looking at possibly replaying it several times. This game's replay-ability isn't great. Not knowing what comes next is really the driving power behind this game, so replaying it isn't nearly as exciting.

I enjoy several game genres, but for a slow, relaxing experience, this type of game suits me best. In the same vein as titles such as Papers, Please and Not Tonight, Orwell does it with a twist. It essentially turns your desktop into the computer of the intelligence gather used in the game.

Orwell, however, is a step up. It's fun, but it's also quite creepy and invites an examination of the risks of our "share everything on the Internet" culture. Is your Facebook account linked to your Instagram account? Is your name on either one the same as the one on your LinkdIn? In Orwell, connections like these allow you, the investigator, to track people across a virtual Internet, constantly digging for more information.

Ethical and moral choices arise. An early one (during the tutorial section, but still a possible spoiler) is the decision between [spoiler] reporting the "friendly" theft of a credit card. Report it and have the card canceled, or don't report it so further card activity can be tracked? [/spoiler]

The game has 2 main problems:
Firstly, all the info/evidences from the sources are highlighted for you!! No need to read much. You just need to click, drag and drop into different profiles. That's your job, I swear! Geez!!

Secondly, when new info/evidence pops up, you can't override the old ones in the Orwell database. What?? Sigh.

At the time of writing, I have yet to finish the game. It's really painful to continue but I will try. In my opinion, totally not worth the time if you really want true blue investigative work. Buy L.A. Noire instead.

Brief overview upon completion:
Overall fantastic experience. The store page doesn't do the game justice. I certainly wouldn't have bought this game had it not been free on Humble Bundle, but now I'm planning on buying the sequel.

- The story is engaging and the "gameplay" of sorts feels satisfying.
- The game is almost entirely story-driven, so replayability is lacking, but that's to be expected.
- The game can be slightly preachy from any perspective, but this likely won't break your involvement in the story.
- The artstyle can be comical at times, but is overall pleasant and non-invasive.
-In-game profile pictures are very limited and many players online have expressed their distaste for the lack of choices. I didn't find them to be appealing either.

Buy this game when it goes on sale if you're unsure of what you'd think of it, but I'd qualify it as worth the $10 base price if it already looks like something you'd enjoy.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.
